reference.source: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies / WHO envenoming guidance
clinicalPearls: Broad syndromes vary by family: elapids (cobras, kraits, mambas, taipans) tend to produce neurotoxic descending paralysis, while vipers cause local cytotoxicity, coagulopathy and haemorrhage
A dry bite (no envenomation) is common; observe for a meaningful period before excluding envenomation, as neurotoxic and coagulation effects may be delayed
Ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, bulbar weakness and progressive respiratory muscle failure are the hallmarks of neurotoxic envenomation and mandate close airway monitoring
Venom-induced consumption coagulopathy (VICC) can render blood incoagulable; a bedside 20-minute whole-blood clotting test is a useful field indicator of systemic viper envenomation
Progressive local swelling, blistering, bruising and tissue necrosis characterise cytotoxic bites and can cause compartment syndrome
Species-appropriate antivenom is the definitive treatment for systemic envenomation; timing, dose to effect and monitoring for anaphylactoid reactions are key principles
Pressure immobilisation is appropriate for neurotoxic elapid and sea-snake bites to delay systemic spread, but is NOT recommended for cytotoxic viper bites where it may worsen local tissue injury
Reassess repeatedly, as neurotoxicity and coagulopathy can evolve or recur and may require repeat antivenom dosing
reference.pathophysiology: Snake venoms are complex mixtures of enzymes and peptides that produce syndrome-specific injury. Pre-synaptic and post-synaptic neurotoxins block neuromuscular transmission to cause a descending flaccid paralysis affecting cranial, bulbar and respiratory muscles. Procoagulant and fibrinolytic components activate the clotting cascade and consume fibrinogen, producing venom-induced consumption coagulopathy with a risk of spontaneous haemorrhage, while haemorrhagins damage vascular endothelium. Cytotoxins, phospholipases and metalloproteinases cause local tissue oedema, blistering and necrosis, and some venoms produce myotoxicity with rhabdomyolysis or systemic capillary leak and shock.
additionalDifferentials: Non-venomous or dry bite with anxiety and local trauma
Other envenomation (scorpion, spider) or arthropod bite
Primary neuromuscular disorder (myasthenic crisis, Guillain-Barre syndrome)
Sepsis or another cause of consumptive coagulopathy
additionalInvestigations: 20-minute whole-blood clotting test at the bedside as a screen for coagulopathy
Full coagulation studies including prothrombin time, fibrinogen and D-dimer
Full blood count for thrombocytopenia and evolving anaemia
Creatine kinase, renal function and urinalysis for rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria
Serial spirometry or forced vital capacity to track neurotoxic respiratory decline
Electrocardiography and continuous monitoring in systemic envenomation
redFlags: Progressive bulbar or respiratory muscle weakness threatening the airway
Spontaneous systemic bleeding or an incoagulable 20-minute clotting test
Rapidly advancing limb swelling with features suggesting compartment syndrome
Shock, oliguria or acute kidney injury
Anaphylactoid reaction to antivenom during infusion
reference.prognosis: With timely species-appropriate antivenom and supportive care including ventilation for neurotoxic paralysis, most patients recover fully. Delayed treatment increases the risk of death from respiratory failure or haemorrhage, and severe cytotoxic bites may leave permanent tissue loss or amputation.
pitfalls: Applying arterial tourniquets or incising/sucking the wound, which increase local tissue damage without benefit
Delaying antivenom in evolving systemic envenomation while awaiting definitive species identification
Discharging early after an apparent dry bite before delayed neurotoxicity or coagulopathy has been excluded
Using pressure immobilisation for cytotoxic viper bites where it aggravates local necrosis
Failing to monitor for and treat recurrent coagulopathy or neurotoxicity after initial improvement
references: WHO Guidelines for the management of snakebite envenoming
management: Administer species-appropriate antivenom titrated to clinical and laboratory effect, with readiness to manage anaphylactoid reactions.
Airway protection and mechanical ventilation for neurotoxic descending paralysis and respiratory muscle failure.
Correct venom-induced consumption coagulopathy with antivenom and blood products such as fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate for active haemorrhage.
Supportive wound care, tetanus prophylaxis and analgesia, while avoiding harmful measures such as tourniquets and incision.
Consider a trial of anticholinesterase, with neostigmine and an antimuscarinic agent, where post-synaptic neurotoxic envenomation is suspected.

Serial monitoring with whole-blood clotting test and coagulation studies, vital capacity, creatine kinase and renal function, with renal replacement therapy for acute kidney injury and fasciotomy for true compartment syndrome.
Escalate to critical care for ventilatory support and management of systemic complications.
